0.title: Song of Songs: Love Strong as Death
0.overview:
The Song of Songs is a love poem. It is the voice of a bride and her bridegroom, delighting in each other, losing and finding each other, and declaring that love is strong as death (8:6). Its title calls it the finest of all songs (1:1).

It is full of gardens, vineyards, spices and doves. It speaks frankly about desire and the body, and it is never crude. The ESV's speaker labels (She, He, Others) are the translators' additions (ESV note). God is named only once (8:6), yet the whole poem is set within his gift of marriage.

The first meaning of the Song is its plain meaning: it celebrates the love of a husband and wife. God made man and woman for each other: they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed (Gen 2:24-25). The Song is that verse set to music, honouring married love, including its physical delight, as the Creator's gift: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4).

The allegorical reading has a long history. Jewish teachers read the Song as the love of God and Israel, and many church fathers and later Christian writers, Bernard of Clairvaux among them, as Christ and the church or the soul. They had reasons in Scripture’s own picture of God as husband. Its weakness is that the book never says it is an allegory, and the details can be made to mean whatever the reader wishes. Many Puritan and Reformed preachers read it chiefly of Christ and the church, with deep comfort. The reading taken here is the plain one first, with the echo of Christ that all marriage carries.

Who wrote it? The title which is Solomon’s (1:1) can mean by, for or about Solomon. Solomon wrote many songs (1 Kgs 4:32), and some suggest it comes from his early years, before his many wives turned his heart; others think another poet wrote of him. Certainty is not possible. Either way, the book holds up the love of one man and one woman, the opposite of Solomon’s later harem.

The Song is a sequence of poems, not a story in strict order, so the embraces of the early chapters need not come before the wedding of 3:6–11.

The Song also guards the gift. Three times the bride charges that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), and she is a garden locked (4:12), opened gladly to her husband (4:16). Desire is honoured by being kept for its time and its covenant, and where it has not been kept, the Bridegroom's love still forgives and makes clean.

Not every reader comes to this book glad. The single who long to marry, the widowed, and those wounded by abuse or betrayal may find it painful. No one is less a Christian for lacking what it describes; abuse is never part of the love it praises, and anyone in danger should seek safety at once. Every believer, married or not, belongs to the Bridegroom whose love the Song echoes.

At its heart is mutual belonging (2:16; 6:3; 7:10), and at its climax, Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it (8:7).

The rest of Scripture shows that marriage itself is a picture. The LORD is Israel's husband (Hos 2:19): as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isa 62:5). Paul quotes Genesis 2 and says, This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Eph 5:32). The Bible ends with a wedding: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready (Rev 19:7).

So the Christian reads the Song in two ways at once, without confusing them: a song about marriage, to be enjoyed by husbands and wives, and, because every true marriage is a small echo of the love of Christ for his church, a song that stirs the heart toward the Bridegroom whose love is stronger than death, who laid down his life for his bride, and who says of her, in the end, there is no flaw in you (4:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of Songs and the First Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the title (v. 1), the Song opens in the middle of desire: the bride longs for her beloved, and the king brings her into his chambers while others rejoice (vv. 2-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The Bible's great love song opens with desire that is honest, joyful and directed to one beloved.

verseByVerse.quote: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Song of Songs is built like "King of kings": the song above all songs. Solomon's songs were 1,005 (1 Kgs 4:32), and this is the one given the title. It is a love song: no law, no history, no prophecy, and God is named only once, in the very flame of the LORD (8:6).

How should a Christian read it? First, as what it plainly is: a celebration of love between husband and wife. God made man and woman for each other, to become one flesh and be naked and not ashamed (Gen 2:24-25), and this book sings of that gift. Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4). A church that is embarrassed by this book has become more prudish than God.

Second, because Scripture says that marriage is a picture of something greater, the Song also lifts our eyes: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Eph 5:32). The Song is not a code in which every detail stands for a doctrine. It is a love song about marriage that, read with the whole Bible, makes the heart long for the love of which all marriage is a picture.
verseByVerse.note: The speaker labels (She, He, Others) are added by translators, who work them out from the Hebrew word forms (ESV note at 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine; your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out; therefore virgins love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him kiss me. The Song begins in the middle of desire, and it is the woman who speaks first. In a world that often treated women as property, the Bible's love song opens with a woman's longing, spoken without shame. She begins speaking about him and ends speaking to him, the way love does when the beloved comes near.

A name in Scripture is character and reputation. His spreads like perfumed oil poured out, and others are drawn too. He is worthy of love, and she knows it.

Many believers reading these lines have thought of the royal bridegroom of Psalm 45, a psalm the New Testament applies to Christ (Heb 1:8-9): You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips (Ps 45:2). Christians have often borrowed her words to say that the love of Christ is better than wine, and that we are drawn to him because his love came first. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers. We will exult and rejoice in you; we will extol your love more than wine; rightly do they love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Draw me after you. She wants him to lead and wants to follow eagerly. Love is not reluctant. The king brings her into his private rooms; to the woman who loves him, her husband is a king.

When the others say We will exult, they show that love between husband and wife is private, and also something the community celebrates, as every wedding feast says.

Christians have long made Draw me after you; let us run their own prayer to Christ. We do not come to him on our own; Jesus said that no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). But when he draws, we run. When did you last run to him, rather than drag your feet?

Is the bridegroom a king or a shepherd? He is called both (v. 4, v. 7). Some see two men, Solomon as a rival to a shepherd lover; others take the bridegroom as Solomon himself. The likeliest reading is that “king” and “shepherd” are two pictures of the same beloved: to her he is royal in honour and close as a shepherd.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bride is self-conscious about her sun-darkened skin, yet says she is lovely (vv. 5-6). She asks where to find her shepherd, and is told to follow the flock (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Love sees and delights in the one who feels unseen and unlovely.

verseByVerse.quote: I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dark, but lovely. Her words to the women of the city carry both embarrassment and confidence. The tents of Kedar were the black goat-hair tents of desert nomads; the curtains of Solomon were rich royal hangings. She is dark like the one, and lovely like the other.

Do not gaze at me. Her angry brothers sent her to labour in the vineyards, and in a court where beauty probably meant pale, pampered skin, she looks like a field worker and has had no time to care for herself. Many know that feeling: the mother who feels she has let herself go, the person shamed by family who carries it into every room.

But she also says but lovely, because her beloved thinks so. Love does not wait for us to become beautiful before it delights in us. The love of Christ is like that. He did not love a church that was already spotless; he loved her so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27). His love makes lovely.

Is this about race? She gives the reason herself: the sun has looked upon me (v. 6), from working outdoors in the vineyards. The Hebrew can be read “dark and lovely”; her unease is about being looked down on as a country labourer, and her answer is that she is lovely. Scripture never treats skin colour as a measure of worth (Acts 17:26).
verseByVerse.note: Kedar was a nomadic tribe of the Arabian desert, known for black goat-hair tents.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions? If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, follow in the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions? You whom my soul loves: the phrase will return again and again (3:1-4). Her beloved is pictured as a shepherd, and she wants to know where to find him at midday rest. She does not want to wander among the other shepherds' flocks like a veiled woman looking for company, a figure who might be mistaken for someone of doubtful reputation. She wants him, and only him.

The answer, follow in the tracks of the flock, comes lightly, perhaps teasingly, and calls her most beautiful among women, the woman who had just asked not to be gazed at.

The shepherd who makes his flock lie down is familiar from the Psalms: He makes me lie down in green pastures (Ps 23:2). And Jesus said, I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). Many Christians have heard a further word here: the soul that loves Christ wants to know where he is, and he is found among his flock, his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Beautiful in Each Other's Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He praises her, she answers with delight in him, and each tells the other, you are beautiful (vv. 9-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Married love is a delight each gives the other in words as well as in presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots. Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. We will make for you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mare among Pharaoh's chariots. His first words are praise. Pharaoh's chariot horses were prized and beautifully adorned, and she stands out like that. She said, Do not gaze at me; he cannot help it.

The promised ornaments show that love pays attention to details, and the gift is for her (the you of verse 11 is feminine singular, ESV note). She came feeling like a field hand; she is treated like a queen.

Husbands can learn from the bridegroom: he speaks his admiration aloud, specifically, and he gives. Many wives have not heard such words in years. A husband who has been cherished by Christ, who speaks delight over a church that did not deserve it, has the best reason and the best help to say them.

verseByVerse.quote: While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of Engedi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answers with fragrance: her love fills the room where the king reclines.

A sachet of myrrh, worn at the breast, keeps its scent close all day and night; so is he to her. Like henna blossoms in the oasis of Engedi, he is refreshment in a dry land.

Twice she says My beloved is to me: not what he is to others, but to her. That is how love speaks. And it is how faith speaks of Christ: not only that he is lovely, but that he is lovely to me, the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Gal 2:20).
verseByVerse.note: Nard was an expensive perfume from India. En-gedi is an oasis by the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves. Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful. Our couch is green; the beams of our house are cedar; our rafters are pine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are beautiful. He says it twice, to the woman who did not want to be looked at. Love repeats itself, because the heart that is loved needs to hear it more than once.

And she says it back. Their love is mutual. Their meeting place seems to be outdoors: the couch is green grass, the rafters cedar and pine. The whole world has become their house.

Here is marriage as God meant it: two people who say, you are beautiful, and mean it, and find that wherever they are together is home. That love has to be tended, as the rest of the Song will show, but it begins in delight given and returned.

1.title: The Song of Songs: Let Him Kiss Me
1.overview: The finest of songs opens with a bride's longing for her bridegroom, spoken first and without shame (vv. 1-4). She feels unlovely, dark from labour in her brothers' vineyards, and wants to know where to find him (vv. 5-8). He answers with praise, and the chapter ends with each telling the other, you are beautiful (vv. 9-17).
1.theology:
God created marriage and the delight of husband and wife, and the Song celebrates that gift without shame (Gen 2:24-25; Heb 13:4). Desire within marriage is good, mutual and to be spoken (vv. 2, 15-16).

Marriage is a picture of Christ and the church (Eph 5:31-32). Read in that light, the Song shows love that comes first and draws the beloved (v. 4; 1 John 4:19), and love that delights in one who feels unlovely and makes her lovely (vv. 5-6, 15; Eph 5:27).
1.examples:
Then: in a world where women were often treated as property, Israel's love song gave the first word to a woman, and let a field-worker who felt unlovely hear herself called the most beautiful among women.

Now: many wives have not heard a specific word of admiration in years, and many people, like the bride, feel they have let themselves go. The Song shows a love that notices, says so aloud, and keeps saying it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — His Banner over Me Was Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She calls herself a simple wildflower, and he calls her a lily among brambles (vv. 1-2). She delights in his shade and fruit (v. 3) and in the banner of his love over her (v. 4). Faint with love, held in his embrace (vv. 5-6), she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Love protects and displays the beloved, and it must be kept for its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys. As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hymns have often sung these words about Christ, but in the Song it is the bride who says them, about herself, and she is not boasting. The flower meant is one of the ordinary wildflowers that covered the coastal plain in spring. She is saying, I am just one flower among thousands.

He turns her modest words around: a lily, but a lily among brambles. To him every other woman is a thorn bush, and she is the one flower. She says, I am ordinary. He says, you are the only one.

That is what love does to a person who thinks little of herself. It does not argue her into self-esteem; it sees her differently and says so. And it is how Christ sees his people: not as one more face in the crowd, but as his own, known by name.
verseByVerse.note: The “rose of Sharon” was probably a bulb such as a crocus or narcissus (ESV note). Sharon is the coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. With great delight I sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answers with a matching picture. Among the forest trees, which give shade but no food, he is an apple tree: shade and fruit together. She rests in his protection and enjoys what he gives. A good husband is both: a shelter his wife can rest under, and a source of delight.

Many believers have found the same double gift, refuge and sweetness, in the Lord. Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him! (Ps 34:8).

verseByVerse.quote: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love. Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The banqueting house is the place of feasting. A banner marked where an army belonged and whose they were; his banner over her, the flag that tells everyone whose she is, is love. When he brings her into company, everyone can see that he loves her. He is not ashamed of her; he displays his love.

Christians have long sung this line of Christ. He has brought his people to his table, and the banner over us is not our record or our achievements, but his love. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8).

She is faint, sick with love, and asks for raisin cakes and apples to revive her. Anyone who has been deeply in love knows the lightheadedness. The Song does not treat that as silly. It is part of the gift.
verseByVerse.note: “Banqueting house” is literally “house of wine” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture is of lovers lying together, his left arm cradling her head, his right arm around her. It is tender and intimate, and the Song does not blush at it. This is the embrace of marriage, and God calls it good.

And immediately a warning, a charge repeated twice more (3:5; 8:4). Having described love's embrace, the bride puts the unmarried young women under oath: do not awaken this before its time.

Sexual love is like a fire. In the hearth of marriage it warms a home; set loose too early, it burns the house down. Do not stir it up by what you watch, read or touch, or where you let your imagination go, before the time God has made for it. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor (1 Thess 4:3-4). This is also a word for the married person tempted to awaken desire for someone who is not his spouse. That will of God is not left to our willpower: the Spirit God gives his people bears the fruit of self-control in them (Gal 5:22-23).

And for those who did not wait, or whose purity was taken from them? Those who have sinned can be washed: such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified (1 Cor 6:11). None of us has kept desire perfectly pure, but Christ did, and his purity is counted to those who trust him. Those who were abused carry no guilt for what was done to them; the shame belongs to the abuser, and Christ receives the wounded with tenderness.

Why swear by the gazelles? They are creatures of grace and beauty, and the oath fits the Song’s world of love; it is a poetic oath, not an appeal to other gods.
verseByVerse.note: “I adjure you” means “I put you under oath” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Arise, My Love, and Come Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He comes leaping over the hills and gazes through the lattice (vv. 8-9). He calls her to come away, for winter is past (vv. 10-13). He longs to see her face and hear her voice (v. 14), and asks that the little foxes be caught (v. 15). My beloved is mine, and I am his (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The beloved comes and calls; love answers, guards what is precious, and rests in mutual belonging.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, looking through the lattice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new scene. She hears his voice before she sees him, and her heart leaps. He is coming, and mountains and hills are nothing to him. Swift and strong like a young stag, he arrives and stands outside, looking in through the lattice. He wants to see her. He will not force the door; he calls.

Many Christians have seen in this a picture of how Christ comes to his people. He does not break down doors. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved speaks and says to me: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His invitation is one of the most beautiful passages in the book: come out of the house; come with me. And the reason is spring. In Israel winter is the season of cold rains; now it is over. Everything is coming to life: flowers, birdsong, figs, vine blossom. Singing may be rendered "pruning", the season when vines are cut back for growth (ESV note). Either way, the world is new, and he wants to enjoy it with her, ending as he began: come away.

Marriages go through winters: seasons of grief, illness, distance, dullness. This is a call to notice when spring comes, and to go out together into it. When did you last say to your husband or wife, come away with me?

And for the believer, a greater spring is coming. The winter of this fallen world will end, and the one who loves his church will call her to come away with him into a world made new.

verseByVerse.quote: O my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the crannies of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is like a dove hiding in a rock crevice, shy, out of reach. He does not drag her out. He tells her what he wants, to see her face and hear her voice, and why: her voice is sweet, her face lovely.

Some people hide from those who love them, afraid to be seen or heard. Love coaxes them out with gentleness and assurance. That is also how the Lord deals with timid hearts. He wants to hear your voice in prayer, not because he needs information, but because he delights in you.

verseByVerse.quote: Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Small animals got into vineyards in spring and destroyed the tender blossoms before the grapes could form. The couple's love is like a vineyard in blossom, and it needs protecting.

It is seldom the great disasters that destroy a marriage. It is the little foxes: the unkind word left unapologised for, the screen that takes the evening, the small resentments, the busyness, the neglect. Catch the foxes for us: it is a shared job. Name the little foxes in your own marriage, or friendship, or walk with God, and catch them before they spoil the fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies. Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on cleft mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the heart of the Song in a single line: mutual belonging. Not ownership in the sense of control, but the covenant belonging of marriage, where each gives himself to the other. He grazes may be rendered "he pastures his flock" (ESV note): he is still the shepherd, among the lilies.

The line will return, reversed, I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (6:3), and again, I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (7:10). First she speaks of possessing him, then of belonging to him, and finally of resting in his desire for her. Love matures from "he is mine" to "I am his".

That is the movement of faith too. The believer begins by rejoicing that Christ is his, and grows into the deeper joy that he belongs to Christ. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14).

Until the morning breeze comes and the night shadows go, she asks him to come to her, swift as a gazelle. Cleft mountains may be rendered "mountains of Bether" (ESV note). The chapter ends with longing for him to be near through the night.

2.title: My Beloved Is Mine, and I Am His
2.overview: Two scenes of love. In the first, the bride and her beloved praise each other, she rests under the banner of his love, and she charges the young women of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time (vv. 1-7). In the second, he comes leaping over the hills to call her out into the spring, and the chapter closes on the line that sums up the whole Song: My beloved is mine, and I am his (vv. 8-17).
2.theology:
Married love is a protecting, public and delighting love (vv. 3-4), and its physical expression is good (v. 6; Heb 13:4). Desire must not be awakened before its time; sexual purity is God's will (v. 7; 1 Thess 4:3-5).

Love must be guarded against small threats (v. 15). Husband and wife belong to each other in covenant (v. 16; 1 Cor 7:4). Christ's love is a banner over his people (v. 4; Rom 5:8); he comes and calls rather than forces (vv. 8-9; Rev 3:20), and his people belong to him (John 10:14).
2.examples: She sees herself as one crocus among thousands on the plain; he sees a lily among brambles. Desire is like fire: in the hearth it warms the house, loose in the house it burns it down. And the foxes that spoil a marriage are usually small, like the screen that quietly takes every evening.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not.<sup>2</sup>I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.<sup>3</sup>The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"<sup>4</sup>Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.<sup>5</sup>I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.<sup>6</sup>What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?<sup>7</sup>Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel,<sup>8</sup>all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.<sup>9</sup>King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon.<sup>10</sup>He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.<sup>11</sup>Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Sought Him Whom My Soul Loves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On her bed by night she seeks him whom my soul loves and does not find him (v. 1). She searches the city and asks the watchmen (vv. 2-3), then finds him and holds him fast (v. 4). Again she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love until it pleases (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Love that has known the beloved cannot rest in his absence; it seeks until it finds and holds fast.

verseByVerse.quote: On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not. I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is night. She reaches for him, and he is not there. Whether this is a dream, a memory of the days before the wedding, or simply the ache of absence, the feeling is plain: longing. Him whom my soul loves appears four times in these four verses; she cannot speak of him without saying how much he means to her.

She does not lie still and wait for the feeling to pass. She goes out into the dark city to look for him, improper as that is for a young woman at night. Love makes people bold.

Believers know nights like this, when the sense of God's nearness is gone. Isaiah prayed it: My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you (Isa 26:9). The right response is not to roll over and wait, but to rise and seek him in his word, in prayer, among his people, the means he has given for finding him.

For the widowed, reaching across the bed and finding no one may be all too literal. The Song does not mock that grief, and the Lord who is near to the brokenhearted (Ps 34:18) does not leave the bereaved alone in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?" Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She does not even explain herself to the watchmen. She simply asks, Have you seen him whom my soul loves?, as if everyone must know who she means. The one who loves assumes the whole world knows the beloved.

And just past them, there he is. She brings him home, into the family house, the place of safety and belonging. Having found him after such a night, she will not lose him again.

Jacob wrestled through the night and said, I will not let you go unless you bless me (Gen 32:26). Mary Magdalene went looking in the dark for the body of her Lord, and when he spoke her name, held on to him, so that he said, Do not cling to me, for he had still to ascend to the Father (John 20:15, 17). The risen Christ is now found by faith, and faith holds him and will not let him go. And beneath that grip is a firmer one: he holds us.

verseByVerse.quote: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refrain of 2:7 returns word for word. After a scene of intense longing, the bride again puts the young women under oath: longing this powerful is exactly why it must not be stirred up before its time.

No book of the Bible celebrates desire more openly than the Song, and it also warns more than once about awakening it too soon. Those who treasure love most will guard it most carefully.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A perfumed procession rises from the wilderness like columns of smoke: Solomon's litter, guarded by sixty mighty men (vv. 6-8), his carriage of cedar, silver, gold and purple, inlaid with love (vv. 9-10). The daughters of Zion are called to see the king crowned on his wedding day (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The wedding day is the king's day of gladness, and all are called out to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new and grand scene. From a distance all anyone can see is smoke rising like pillars, and all anyone can smell is myrrh, frankincense and costly spices. A procession is coming.

For Israelite ears, a column rising from the wilderness might recall the pillar of cloud that led their fathers through the desert. That may be only an echo, but it lends the moment a sense of glory: something wonderful is on the way.

Who is in the litter? The king arrives in splendour on his wedding day (v. 11), with the bride most likely carried in procession. It is a picture of the royal honour of the wedding, whether or not one takes it of Solomon’s own marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel, all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Around the king's litter march sixty warriors, the best of Israel's soldiers, a royal wedding procession. They are armed against terror by night: bandits on the road, attackers in the dark. The king protects what he loves. A husband who loves his wife makes her safe.

The same phrase appears in a psalm of God's protection over his people: You will not fear the terror of the night (Ps 91:5).
verseByVerse.note: A “litter” is a couch carried by servants (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Carriage may be rendered "sedan chair" (ESV note). It was made of cedar from Lebanon, the finest timber of the ancient world, the wood of the temple itself, with silver posts, a gold back, a purple seat. And the inside was inlaid with love by the women of the city, perhaps with embroidery made as a wedding gift. The most beautiful thing about the carriage was not the gold but the love worked into it.

A home can be furnished with silver and gold and still be cold. What makes the inside beautiful is love worked into it, day by day, by the people who live there.

verseByVerse.quote: Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king wears a wedding crown given by his mother, and the day is called the day of the gladness of his heart. Of all the days of Solomon's reign, with its wealth and wisdom and temple building, this one is named as the day his heart was glad. Psalm 45 describes a royal wedding in the same spirit, where the bride is led to the king with joy and gladness (Ps 45:14-15).

And Scripture points to another Bridegroom and another wedding. Jesus spoke of the cry at midnight, Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him (Matt 25:6). The only crown this King was given on earth was from soldiers: the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head (John 19:2). Yet even that day had a gladness hidden in it. He went to the cross for the joy that was set before him (Heb 12:2), the joy of a Bridegroom winning his bride. Scripture's last pages speak of the marriage of the Lamb (Rev 19:7), and on that day the gladness of his heart will be complete.

3.title: Him Whom My Soul Loves
3.overview: The chapter moves from the dark to the light. First a night of longing: the bride searches the city for him whom my soul loves, finds him and will not let him go, and again warns against awakening love before its time (vv. 1-5). Then broad day and a royal wedding procession, as the king comes up from the wilderness in splendour, crowned on the day of the gladness of his heart (vv. 6-11).
3.theology:
True love seeks the beloved in his absence and holds fast when he is found (vv. 1-4); the believer seeks the Lord in seasons when he seems far (Isa 26:9). Desire must still be kept for its time (v. 5).

Marriage is a day of royal joy, and a husband protects and honours his bride (vv. 6-11). The wedding of the king points to Christ the Bridegroom (Matt 25:6), who wore a crown of thorns for the joy set before him (John 19:2; Heb 12:2) and will rejoice over his bride.
3.examples: Anyone who has reached across the bed in the dark and found no one knows the ache of these verses. And anyone who has stood on a station platform scanning the crowd for one face knows the joy of the moment she finds him.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.<sup>2</sup>Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young.<sup>3</sup>Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.<sup>4</sup>Your neck is like the tower of David, built in rows of stone; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors.<sup>5</sup>Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.<sup>6</sup>Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go away to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense.<sup>7</sup>You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.<sup>8</sup>Come with me from Lebanon, my bride; come with me from Lebanon. Depart from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.<sup>9</sup>You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; you have captivated my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace.<sup>10</sup>How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!<sup>11</sup>Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.<sup>12</sup>A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed.<sup>13</sup>Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with all choicest fruits, henna with nard,<sup>14</sup>nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all choice spices—<sup>15</sup>a garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon.<sup>16</sup>Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind! Blow upon my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He praises her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, cheeks and neck, and her breasts like twin fawns (vv. 1-5). He will go to the mountain of myrrh until the day breathes (v. 6). You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The bridegroom's love sees the whole of his bride, and to him she is without flaw.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the wedding night, or near it, and the bridegroom begins as in chapter 1: you are beautiful. Then he takes his time, praising his bride from her eyes downward, one feature at a time. Love does not glance. It gazes, and it names what it sees.

Her eyes are doves behind her veil, glimpsed, gentle, bright.

To our ears, goats are not flattering. But picture a flock of black goats flowing down a far hillside in the evening light, a dark wave rippling over the slope. That is her long dark hair as it moves. In the shepherd's world of the Song it is the highest compliment.

verseByVerse.quote: Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Freshly washed sheep, each paired with its twin: her teeth are white, even and complete, none missing. In a world without dentists, that was a real beauty. Red lips like a scarlet cord; cheeks flushed like a cut pomegranate. Every line is specific. The bridegroom has paid attention.

Husbands can copy his method: notice, then say it. Most spouses long to hear specific praise far more often than they do. Generic compliments are easy. Detailed delight takes attention, and attention is a form of love.

verseByVerse.quote: Your neck is like the tower of David, built in rows of stone; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her neck is tall and straight, adorned with necklaces like shields hung on a fortress wall (the Hebrew behind rows of stone is uncertain). She carries herself like a queen.

The praise of her breasts is frank and tender: fawns are soft, gentle and lovely. Scripture is not embarrassed by a husband's delight in his wife's body; Proverbs commands it: rejoice in the wife of your youth (Prov 5:18). The same Bible that forbids lust outside marriage celebrates desire within it. The difference is not the body or the desire, which God made. It is the covenant. Inside it, this kind of praise is holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go away to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense. You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He echoes her words from 2:17, Until the day breathes and the shadows flee. Where she had asked him to come to her through the night, he now says he will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense, fragrant heights that in the poem seem to picture his bride herself.

No flaw in you. Of course she had flaws; the woman of chapter 1 knew it well. But this is how a loving husband sees his wife: not blind to reality, but seeing her as a whole through the eyes of love, and delighting in the whole.

And here the Song reaches toward something only the gospel can make fully true. Of his church, which is anything but flawless now, Christ intends that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish (Eph 5:27). He has reconciled us in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him (Col 1:22). What the bridegroom says in love, Christ will one day make literally so: there is no flaw in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — A Garden Locked, a Fountain Sealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He calls his bride from Lebanon (v. 8); she has captivated his heart, and her love is better than wine (vv. 9-11). She is a garden locked, a sealed fountain full of choice fruits and spices (vv. 12-15), and she opens it to him: Let my beloved come to his garden (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride keeps herself for her husband alone, and gives herself to him freely and gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride; come with me from Lebanon. Depart from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the first time he calls her my bride, a word he uses five times in verses 8-12. He calls her away from the high, wild mountains of the north, places of lions and leopards. Depart may be rendered "Look" (ESV note). Either way, he calls her from what is remote, dangerous and lonely, to himself.

Marriage calls a person out of the old life into a new one, as the Lord calls his people out of the old life to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; you have captivated my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace. How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice! Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Sister" here is not a word of blood but of closeness: she is family to him, bound to him for life, not merely desired. One glance, one jewel on her necklace, and the king is undone.

In chapter 1 she said your love is better than wine (1:2). Now he says the same to her. The love that began with her longing is fully returned.

Honey and milk are the words of the promised land. His bride is a promised land to him, sweetness and plenty, in her kisses and in her words.

verseByVerse.quote: A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three pictures of one truth: a locked garden, a private spring, a sealed fountain. She has kept herself for him. Her body and her love were not open to anyone who passed by.

Proverbs uses the same imagery for faithfulness in marriage: Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well, Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth (Prov 5:15, 18). The locked garden is chastity before marriage and faithfulness within it.

In a culture where the gate is left open, that sounds restrictive. The Song presents it as the opposite: what is given to everyone is given to no one in particular; what is kept for one can be given to him wholly. If you have not kept the gate, the gospel does not leave you locked out. Christ cleanses and restores, and the bride he presents is made pure by him.
verseByVerse.note: The garden returns in 5:1 and 6:2, where the beloved has come into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with all choicest fruits, henna with nard, nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all choice spices— a garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind the locked gate is a paradise: pomegranates and every choice fruit, and spices from across the known world, nard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh, aloes. No single garden could grow them all. The bride is every delight in one. And she is a well of living water, fresh and flowing, a spring that keeps refreshing her husband.

The phrase living water points beyond. God called himself the fountain of living waters (Jer 2:13), and Jesus promised, Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water' (John 7:38). Without making the bride's garden a code, Christians may rejoice that the church, filled with his Spirit, becomes a spring that refreshes others.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind! Blow upon my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the bride speaks, and her answer is the climax of the chapter. She calls on the winds to carry her garden's fragrance to him. And then the lovely change of pronoun: my garden becomes his garden. The locked garden is opened, freely, to the one it was kept for.

This is the consummation of the marriage, told with delicacy and joy. Chastity was never meant to be a closed gate forever. It was keeping the garden for this.

Many Christians have also prayed these words of Christ. The believer's heart belongs to him. When the Spirit blows on it, the spices flow, and the fruit is his: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22-23). Can you pray the bride's prayer? Let my beloved come to his garden.

4.title: You Are Altogether Beautiful, My Love
4.overview: The wedding night. The bridegroom praises his bride from head to heart and calls her altogether beautiful (vv. 1-7). Then he calls her to himself as my bride, and pictures her as a locked garden kept for him alone, which she gladly opens to him (vv. 8-16).
4.theology:
Delight in a spouse's body and person is good and holy within marriage (vv. 1-7; Prov 5:18-19; Heb 13:4). Chastity before marriage and faithfulness within it keep love for one person, to be given wholly and gladly (vv. 12, 16; Prov 5:15-18; 1 Cor 7:2).

The bridegroom's no flaw in you (v. 7) anticipates Christ presenting his church without spot or blemish (Eph 5:27; Col 1:22). God is the fountain of living waters, and those who believe in Christ become sources of living water and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 15-16; John 7:38; Gal 5:22-23).
4.examples: A husband who says "you look nice" has paid a compliment; one who notices how her eyes catch the light when she laughs has paid attention, and that is what this chapter teaches. And a garden gate kept locked through years of waiting is not a loss but a gift, kept for the day it is opened gladly.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey, I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!<sup>2</sup>I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking. "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."<sup>3</sup>I had put off my garment; how could I put it on? I had bathed my feet; how could I soil them?<sup>4</sup>My beloved put his hand to the latch, and my heart was thrilled within me.<sup>5</sup>I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.<sup>6</sup>I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.<sup>7</sup>The watchmen found me as they went about in the city; they beat me, they bruised me, they took away my veil, those watchmen of the walls.<sup>8</sup>I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him I am sick with love.<sup>9</sup>What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you thus adjure us?<sup>10</sup>My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand.<sup>11</sup>His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven.<sup>12</sup>His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting beside a full pool.<sup>13</sup>His cheeks are like beds of spices, mounds of sweet-smelling herbs. His lips are lilies, dripping liquid myrrh.<sup>14</sup>His arms are rods of gold, set with jewels. His body is polished ivory, bedecked with sapphires.<sup>15</sup>His legs are alabaster columns, set on bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.<sup>16</sup>His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bridegroom answers his bride's invitation and comes to his garden, and a voice blesses the couple (v. 1).
verseByVerse.theology: The consummation of marriage is received as a feast, and blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey, I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of chapter 4 the bride said, Let my beloved come to his garden. Here is his answer, and every line is my: my myrrh, my honeycomb, my wine. What she kept for him is now his, and he receives it with delight. The poem tells the wedding night with great restraint and great joy.

Then a voice blesses them, the wedding guests or the poet himself, standing back. The message is clear: this is good. Enjoy it fully. Scripture forbids drunkenness with wine (Eph 5:18), and here it urges a husband and wife to be overcome with love for each other.

The Christian church has sometimes spoken about sex in marriage as if it were a concession. Verse 1 speaks of it as a feast, and blesses it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Half-asleep, she hears her beloved knocking (v. 2), but hesitates (v. 3). When at last she rises to open, he has gone (vv. 4-6). Searching the city, she is beaten by the watchmen (v. 7), and charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him I am sick with love (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Even real love can grow slow to respond, and the cost of delay is felt in the beloved's absence.

verseByVerse.quote: I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking. "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new scene, and a painful one. She is dozing at night when her husband knocks. He calls her by four names of love, wet with the dew of the night, wanting to come in to her. Nothing in his words is harsh or demanding. It is a tender invitation.

The picture of a beloved knocking at the door has entered Christian devotion through the words of the risen Christ to a lukewarm church: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev 3:20).

Is this a dream? I slept, but my heart was awake suggests a dream or half-dream, as in 3:1–4. Either way, the point holds: love that is slow to answer can find the beloved gone, and must go out to seek him.

Is it wrong for a spouse to refuse the other? Weariness and seasons happen, and the lover here does not force or demand. But habitual refusal harms a marriage: husband and wife are to give themselves to each other, and not to deprive one another except by agreement for a time (1 Cor 7:3–5).

verseByVerse.quote: I had put off my garment; how could I put it on? I had bathed my feet; how could I soil them? My beloved put his hand to the latch, and my heart was thrilled within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her excuses are small: undressed, feet washed. She is not refusing him. She is simply not bothered enough, just now, to get up.

Every married person knows this moment. It is not rejection. It is the slow drift of comfort, tiredness and self-concern that leaves a spouse knocking. Most marriages that cool do not end in a great quarrel. They end in a long series of doors not opened.

He tries the latch, and her heart leaps. She does love him. But feeling alone has not yet got her out of bed.

The same drift happens in the life of faith. Christ calls, through his word, a stirring in the conscience, an opportunity to pray or serve, and we stay where we are. Jesus told his disciples to be ready to open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks (Luke 12:36). None of us has always answered at once. He did, always doing what pleased his Father, and in him our slowness is forgiven; the Spirit who stirred her heart stirs ours to rise and open.

verseByVerse.quote: I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the bolt. I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At last she gets up. On the bolt she finds myrrh, perhaps left by him as a token, perhaps her own, put on for him. And he is gone. Remembering his words now pierces her. She searches and calls, and there is no answer.

This is not a husband sulking. He did not break the door down, and he did not wait forever. The Song shows, simply, that delay has a cost. Opportunities for love do not stay open indefinitely.

Believers can know a season when the sense of the Lord's nearness is withdrawn after we have been slow to respond. The psalmist prayed in such a season, Restore to me the joy of your salvation (Ps 51:12). The Lord does not abandon his own, but he may let us feel the absence we chose so that we learn to seek him. And the promise stands: You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart (Jer 29:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The watchmen found me as they went about in the city; they beat me, they bruised me, they took away my veil, those watchmen of the walls. I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In chapter 3 the watchmen let her pass. This time they beat her and strip her veil. The Song does not explain why. It tells the truth that love sometimes seeks through pain, and that those who should protect do not always do so.

Bruised, she does not give up or grow bitter. The words she used in 2:5, faint with the joy of his presence, she now uses in the pain of his absence. Her love has not changed, only her circumstances. That is a mark of real love, and real faith: it longs for the beloved as much in his absence as in his presence.

Does the Song approve the beating? No. It reports a wrong done to her, as Scripture reports many wrongs, and it does not blame her for it. Nothing here excuses violence against a woman, in the street or in a home; anyone being hurt should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asked what makes her beloved more than another (v. 9), she praises him from head to foot (vv. 10-15): he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: When asked what makes her beloved different, the bride can describe him in detail, and her delight is her testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you thus adjure us?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The daughters of Jerusalem ask it twice: every woman has a beloved; what makes yours special?

It is the question the world asks the church. You speak of Jesus as if he were more than any other teacher, any other hope, any other love. The bride's answer, which follows, is the model for ours.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand. His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting beside a full pool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She does not argue. She describes him. Radiant and ruddy: glowing with health and life. Distinguished among ten thousand: pick him out of any crowd. The only full description of the bridegroom in the Song is given when he is absent, and she is asked why she loves him.

Her praise moves from his head downward, as his praise of her did in chapter 4: a head like finest gold, thick dark hair. He had said her eyes were doves (4:1); she says the same of his, the whites clear as if bathed in milk (the Hebrew here is uncertain, but the picture of peace and beauty is plain).

verseByVerse.quote: His cheeks are like beds of spices, mounds of sweet-smelling herbs. His lips are lilies, dripping liquid myrrh. His arms are rods of gold, set with jewels. His body is polished ivory, bedecked with sapphires. His legs are alabaster columns, set on bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His face is fragrant; his words are sweet as myrrh, as lovely as how he looks. Strong arms like golden rods, a body like polished ivory, sapphires (in Hebrew "lapis lazuli"); legs like marble pillars, tall as the cedars of Lebanon. She describes him like a precious statue, splendid from head to foot.

A Christian reading this cannot help asking: could I describe my Lord with half this delight? Scripture gives us far more to say than she had. He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:3), the image of the invisible God (Col 1:15), and the most handsome of the sons of men, with grace poured upon your lips (Ps 45:2). Many believers can explain doctrines about Christ, and few can describe him with this kind of love. The Song teaches us to try.

verseByVerse.quote: His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mouth is in Hebrew "palate": his kisses and his words are sweetness itself. As he called her altogether beautiful (4:7), she calls him altogether desirable. There is nothing about him she would change.

Her final words are the simplest and perhaps the deepest: my beloved and my friend. The best marriages are both, passion and friendship together, and friendship carries a marriage through the long years when passion ebbs and flows.

Jesus offers his people the same double gift. He is the Bridegroom, and he says, I have called you friends (John 15:15). Paul, who had lost everything, counted it all as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8). That is what it sounds like when someone finds a beloved who is altogether desirable. Can you say of him, this is my beloved, and this is my friend?

5.title: This Is My Beloved and This Is My Friend
5.overview: The chapter opens on the wedding feast, blessed by a voice that calls it good (v. 1). Then comes a night of slowness and loss: the bride is slow to open to her beloved, finds him gone, and searches at real cost (vv. 2-8). Asked what makes him worth it, she answers with the fullest portrait of him in the Song: This is my beloved and this is my friend (vv. 9-16).
5.theology:
The consummation of marriage is a blessed feast (v. 1; Heb 13:4). Love must be tended; slowness to respond, even without hostility, has real costs (vv. 2-6; Luke 12:36), and those who have drifted are called to seek again with the whole heart (Jer 29:13; Ps 51:12).

Love is shown by delight in the beloved and by the ability to describe him (vv. 10-16). Christ is the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), altogether desirable to those who know him (Phil 3:8), and both Bridegroom and friend (John 15:15).
5.examples: Ask a widow about the husband she lost, and she will not give you a list of his opinions; her face changes and she describes him. That is what the bride does when the world asks, "What is your beloved more than another?", and it is what the church is asked to do for Christ.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?<sup>2</sup>My beloved has gone down to his garden to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.<sup>3</sup>I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.<sup>4</sup>You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.<sup>5</sup>Turn away your eyes from me, for they overwhelm me— Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.<sup>6</sup>Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins; not one among them has lost its young.<sup>7</sup>Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.<sup>8</sup>There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and virgins without number.<sup>9</sup>My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines also, and they praised her.<sup>10</sup>"Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?"<sup>11</sup>I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.<sup>12</sup>Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince.<sup>13</sup>Return, return, O Shulammite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon a dance before two armies?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Where Has Your Beloved Gone?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moved by her description, the daughters of Jerusalem ask where he has gone, that they may seek him with her (v. 1). She knows: he has gone down to his garden. I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (vv. 2-3).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride's delight in her beloved makes others want to seek him, and in his absence she rests in belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A remarkable change. In 5:9 the daughters of Jerusalem asked, with some doubt, what made her beloved special. Now they are not asking why but where. Her description has made them want him too.

That is how people are drawn to Christ: not usually by argument first, but by hearing someone who loves him describe him. When believers speak of their Lord with delight, others begin to ask where he may be found.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved has gone down to his garden to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies. I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In chapter 5 she searched the city in vain. Now she answers without hesitation: in his garden. And in the Song the garden is his bride herself (4:12, 16; 5:1). He has gone where he belongs, to her. To graze may be rendered "to pasture his flock" (ESV note): the shepherd is among his lilies.

The words of 2:16 return, but reversed. There she said, My beloved is mine, and I am his. Now, after the night of loss, she begins with his claim on her. When she felt most unsure of her grip on him, she rested in his grip on her.

That is the comfort of the believer in a season of spiritual dryness. Feelings of nearness come and go. The covenant does not: I am my beloved's. Jesus said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — My Dove, My Perfect One, Is the Only One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He greets her without reproach and repeats his earlier praise almost word for word (vv. 4-7). Among sixty queens and eighty concubines she is the only one, and even the queens praise her (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Love restored speaks the same words it spoke before, and to the husband his wife is the only one.

verseByVerse.quote: You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the scene of the closed door, the reader might expect reproach. There is none; his first words are praise. She is beautiful as Tirzah, a city famous for its beauty and for a time a royal capital of the northern kingdom, and lovely as Jerusalem, the city of God.

And awesome as an army with banners: her beauty is not only gentle but majestic, like a great army marching with its standards raised. A husband who loves his wife is not only charmed by her. He is in awe of her.
verseByVerse.note: Tirzah (its name suggests "pleasing") later served as an early capital of the northern kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn away your eyes from me, for they overwhelm me— Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins; not one among them has lost its young. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her eyes overwhelm him, as in 4:9. And these lines are almost exactly the words he spoke in 4:1-3, before the door was left closed. He does not compose new, cooler praise. Her hesitation has not changed how he sees her.

That is what forgiveness looks like in a marriage. Not "I will love you again when you have earned it", but the same words, the same delight, restored. And it is how Christ restores his people. After Peter denied him, the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61-62). But the risen Lord did not give Peter a lesser place. He gave him back his calling.

verseByVerse.quote: There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and virgins without number. My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines also, and they praised her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king's palace was full of women. He could have anyone. And yet, twice: the only one. Among all the women he could have, she is the one. That is the shape of love as God designed it: one man, one woman, each the only one to the other. They shall become one flesh. The Song lifts up this ideal even though the kings of Israel, Solomon among them, so often fell short of it.

And the other women do not resent her; they praise her. Christians have seen in this a picture of the church, loved by Christ as his only bride, whose good life even a hostile world sometimes cannot help admiring (1 Pet 2:12).

Sixty queens and eighty concubines are far fewer than the 700 wives and 300 concubines of 1 Kings 11:3, perhaps because the Song comes from earlier in Solomon’s reign, or because the numbers are poetic. Does the Bible approve of such a harem? No. It records polygamy without commending it, the law forbade the king to multiply wives (Deut 17:17), and Solomon’s wives turned his heart away (1 Kgs 11:4). The Song itself sets the one beloved above them all.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
These seem to be the words of the queens and the young women, reaching for the largest pictures they have: dawn, moon, sun, a marching army.

The woman of chapter 1 said, Do not gaze at me because I am dark (1:6). Now she is bright as the sun. That is what love has done for her. A bride who is truly loved begins to shine. And Jesus promised that the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt 13:43).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She went down to the nut orchard, and her desire carried her among the chariots of a prince (vv. 11-12). The others call, Return, return, O Shulammite (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride is named, called back and admired; love's joy draws others to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom. Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spring in the Song is the season of love (2:11-13), and the garden is the place of love.

Verse 12 is one of the hardest in the Song, and should be held lightly. The last phrase may be rendered "chariots of Ammi-Nadib", which could be a name (ESV note). The general sense seems to be that, before she knew it, her desire carried her away into a place of honour, as if swept up into a royal chariot beside her prince. Love surprised her and lifted her up.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, return, O Shulammite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon a dance before two armies?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the first and only time the bride has a name, or a title: the Shulammite. The others call her back four times because they want to see her. Someone answers, perhaps the bride, perhaps the bridegroom: why gaze on her as upon a dance before two armies (or "dance of Mahanaim")? It seems to picture a festive dance that draws every eye, and the next chapter begins his praise of her as she dances.

The woman who did not want to be looked at in chapter 1 is now the one everyone wants to see. Christians have sometimes borrowed the chorus Return, return as a call to anyone who has wandered: come back, so that we may see you again among us.
verseByVerse.note: Song 6:13 is 7:1 in Hebrew (ESV note). “Shulammite” may mean “the perfect one” or be a feminine echo of Solomon’s name.

6.title: I Am My Beloved's and My Beloved Is Mine
6.overview: After the night of loss in chapter 5, this is a chapter of restoration. The bride's description of her beloved makes others want to seek him, and she rests in belonging to him (vv. 1-3). He greets her without a word of reproach, and to him she is still the only one (vv. 4-10). The chapter ends with the bride lifted up by love and everyone calling her back so that they may see her (vv. 11-13).
6.theology:
Delight in the beloved draws others to seek him (v. 1); the church's love for Christ is part of its witness. In seasons of absence, the believer rests in belonging to the Lord (v. 3; John 6:37).

Love restored speaks the same words as before; forgiveness does not demote the forgiven (vv. 5-7; Luke 22:61-62). God's design for marriage is one man and one woman, each the only one to the other (vv. 8-9; Gen 2:24). The loved bride shines (v. 10), as Christ's church will.
6.examples: After a quarrel, a husband who says the same loving words he said the week before, without a cooler edge, has shown what forgiveness is. And on the days when you cannot feel that Christ is yours, you can still rest in the fact that you are his.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand.<sup>2</sup>Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.<sup>3</sup>Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.<sup>4</sup>Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.<sup>5</sup>Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.<sup>6</sup>How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights!<sup>7</sup>Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.<sup>8</sup>I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples,<sup>9</sup>and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.<sup>10</sup>I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.<sup>11</sup>Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages;<sup>12</sup>let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.<sup>13</sup>The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — How Beautiful and Pleasant You Are
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bridegroom praises his bride from her feet upward (vv. 1-5): How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! (v. 6). He will climb the palm tree to take its fruit, and her mouth is like the best wine (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Delight in one's own spouse, spoken openly and specifically, is a gift of God and a duty of love.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand. Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In chapter 4 he praised her from her eyes downward. Here he begins at her feet, apparently watching the dance of 6:13.

He calls her O noble daughter, a king's word of honour, and says her thighs are the work of a master hand. That is a quiet act of worship. Her body is craftsmanship, and someone made it. The psalmist says the same of himself: I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made (Ps 139:14).

A bowl of wine and a heap of wheat, the two staples of a feast: she is nourishment and celebration to him. The images are agricultural because the Song comes from a farming world, and they are meant warmly: abundance, plenty, harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He repeats the picture of 4:5 and adds new ones. Her neck is an ivory tower, pale and stately. Her eyes are still pools at the city gate, where people lingered. Her nose is like a watchtower: strong, well set, noble, a strange compliment to modern ears, but high praise in a world that prized a straight, strong profile.

Her head is carried like Carmel rising green above the sea. Her hair is dark as royal purple, and in it the king is a prisoner. He has an army, a throne and a palace, and he is captured by his wife's hair. That is how he wants it. Again he names what he sees, because love that is awake pays attention.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With all your delights may be rendered "among delights" (ESV note). She is beautiful and she is pleasant: lovely to look at and lovely to be with. Beauty without pleasantness soon wears thin, and pleasantness makes beauty last.

She is tall and graceful as a date palm, the tree of the oasis: shade, sweetness and life in a dry land.

verseByVerse.quote: I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples, and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having compared her to a palm, he says he will climb it. The Song does not pretend that desire is polite. It is frank, and it is directed entirely to his own wife. That is the point. The same Bible that says everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28) gives a husband these words for his own bride.

The last clause is difficult: the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate read as the ESV does, while the Hebrew reads "causing the lips of sleepers to speak" (ESV note). Her kiss is like the best wine, and it is his.
