Then the speaker changes: for my beloved. In the middle of his praise she answers, taking his words into her own mouth. They are no longer two voices taking turns. They finish each other's lines.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — Come, My Beloved, Let Us Go Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (v. 10). She invites him out to the fields and vineyards, where she will give him her love (vv. 11-12), and has laid up choice fruits for him, new and old (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Mature love rests in being desired and takes the initiative in giving itself.

verseByVerse.quote: I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refrain comes for the third and last time, changed again. In 2:16 she said, My beloved is mine, and I am his. In 6:3, after the night she lost him, she began with belonging. Now she says only the second half, and adds something new: his desire is for me.

That is where love arrives when it matures. Not "he is mine", asserting a claim. Not even "I am his", stating a duty. But resting in the settled knowledge that he wants her. A wife who knows her husband desires her, and a husband who knows his wife delights in him, can weather a great deal.

And it is where the soul arrives with God. The believer's peace is not finally in the strength of his grip on Christ, but in knowing that Christ desires him. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isa 62:5). Can you say it: his desire is for me?

For the single, the widowed, or anyone who has never heard a human voice say this, that comfort is not second best. Christ's desire is for every one of his people, married or not, and it does not fade.
verseByVerse.note: “Desire” is the same Hebrew word as in Genesis 3:16; there it marks conflict after the fall, here love restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages; let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now she takes the initiative. In chapter 2 he said, Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away. Now she says it to him. (In the villages may be rendered "among the henna plants".) Either way, she wants to get away with him.

She plans it: out early, to the vineyards, to see the spring, and there she will give him her love. Desire in marriage is not only the husband's to express, and it is always given, never demanded or forced. Paul says as much: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband (1 Cor 7:3).

Love also needs occasions made for it. They go out early, away from the house and the work, to a place they both love. Marriages are kept alive by such plans.

verseByVerse.quote: The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mandrakes were associated with love and fertility; Rachel and Leah once quarrelled over them (Gen 30:14).

Then the loveliest phrase: new as well as old, which I have laid up for you. A marriage that lasts has both: new joys, and the treasured old ones, the remembered honeymoon, the family jokes, the hard years survived together. Nothing is wasted; everything is laid up for the beloved.

What have you laid up for your husband or wife, and when did you last bring it out? And what have you laid up for the Lord, who receives every act of love done in his name, new and old alike?
verseByVerse.note: The mandrake is a low plant whose small yellow fruit has a strong, sweet scent.

7.title: His Desire Is for Me
7.overview: As the bride dances, the bridegroom praises her from her feet upward, and his frank delight is directed wholly to his own wife (vv. 1-9). Then she speaks the Song's refrain for the last time, in its deepest form, his desire is for me, and takes the initiative in inviting him away to the vineyards (vv. 10-13).
7.theology:
The body is God's craftsmanship, and delight in one's own spouse is holy (vv. 1-9; Ps 139:14; Heb 13:4). Such desire is directed to one's spouse alone, in contrast to lust (Matt 5:28).

Mature love rests in being desired (v. 10), as faith rests in Christ's love for us rather than in the strength of our love for him (1 John 4:19; Isa 62:5). Love is mutual in its initiative and its giving (vv. 11-13; 1 Cor 7:3-4).
7.examples: A king with an army and a throne is held captive by his wife's hair, and is glad of it. A couple long married still finish each other's sentences. And a wife who books a weekend away is doing what the bride does in verse 11: making an occasion for love instead of waiting for one.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh that you were like a brother to me who nursed at my mother's breasts! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and none would despise me.<sup>2</sup>I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother— she who used to teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranate.<sup>3</sup>His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me!<sup>4</sup>I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.<sup>5</sup>Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor.<sup>6</sup>Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.<sup>8</sup>We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for?<sup>9</sup>If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver, but if she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.<sup>10</sup>I was a wall, and my breasts were like towers; then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace.<sup>11</sup>Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard to keepers; each one was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver.<sup>12</sup>My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.<sup>13</sup>O you who dwell in the gardens, with companions listening for your voice; let me hear it.<sup>14</sup>Make haste, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Oh That You Were Like a Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She wishes she could show her love openly and bring him into her mother's house (vv. 1-2). His embrace is as it was (v. 3), and for the third time she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love until it pleases (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Love longs to be public as well as private, and still guards its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you were like a brother to me who nursed at my mother's breasts! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and none would despise me. I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother— she who used to teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In her world a woman could kiss a brother in the street and no one would think anything of it; to kiss a husband in public would be scandalous. So she wishes, oddly and touchingly, that he were her brother, not instead of her husband, but so that her love could be shown anywhere.

Love wants to be open. Something is wrong when a marriage is affectionate behind closed doors and cold in company.

She would bring him home, to the house where she was taught, and give him her best: spiced wine, pomegranate juice. Love gives what it has.

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of 2:6 return, unchanged. Whatever has happened in between, the closed door, the night search, the beating, the embrace is the same: after everything, here they still are.

And the refrain for the third time (2:7; 3:5), the most repeated sentence in the book. A book this frank about desire says three times: do not awaken it before its time. The two are not in tension. Only what is precious needs guarding, and the Song is about to tell us how strong this love is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She comes up from the wilderness leaning on her beloved (v. 5). Set me as a seal upon your heart, for love is strong as death, its flame the very flame of the LORD (v. 6). Many waters cannot quench it, and no wealth can buy it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The Song's climax: love that death cannot break, floods cannot drown and money cannot buy, because its flame is from the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A question from onlookers, echoing 3:6, where a royal procession came up from the wilderness in clouds of perfume. This time it is a woman walking, leaning on her beloved. The grandeur has become intimacy: two people coming home from the wilderness, and she is leaning on him.

That image has comforted Christians for centuries, and rightly, because the pilgrim's journey through the wilderness of this world is made leaning on Christ. But the picture is already tender at the human level: the strength a husband and wife become to each other over years.

Under the apple tree, where love was awakened, is the very place where his mother gave birth to him. Life and love belong to the same ground: marriage is where new life comes from, and every beloved was once someone's newborn child.

Who speaks in “under the apple tree I awakened you”? Most likely the bride, recalling where their love began. The word echoes the refrain about awakening love: here love has been awakened in its proper season.

verseByVerse.quote: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the summit of the Song. A seal was a signet, a ring or cylinder that carried a person's name and stamped his documents; to wear one was to carry an identity. Let me be what you carry closest, on the heart, where love is felt, and on the arm, where it is seen and where it works. Israel was told to bind God's words on the hand (Deut 6:8), and the high priest carried the names of the tribes on his heart when he went in before God (Exod 28:29).

Why does she ask it? Because love is that serious. Strong as death. Nothing in human experience is as irresistible as death; it takes everyone, and no one refuses it. Love is like that, the poem says: it lays hold of a person and will not let go. And jealousy is fierce as the grave: the ESV notes that jealousy may be rendered "ardor", and that the grave is in Hebrew "as Sheol". This is not petty suspicion. It is the rightful passion of love that will not share the beloved. Love by its nature is exclusive.

And here, probably for the only time in the book, God is named. The Hebrew word ends in -yah, a short form of the LORD's name. It may only mean a mighty flame (so the KJV, a most vehement flame), but many think the name is meant, and the ESV takes it so. If it is, that single phrase tells us where this fire comes from. Human love is not merely a chemical accident or a social arrangement. It burns with a flame kindled from the love of God himself. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

And here the Song reaches farthest toward Christ. Paul says that marriage was made to picture Christ and the church (Eph 5:25–32), and Christ's love was in fact strong as death, and stronger. He went into death for his bride and came back. He carries his people as a seal: Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands (Isa 49:16). And he has sealed them to himself: believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Eph 1:13).
verseByVerse.note: On the seal as a sign of belonging, compare Haggai 2:23, where the LORD makes Zerubbabel like a signet ring.

verseByVerse.quote: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire is put out by water; this fire is not. Pour the sea on it and it burns. That is a promise to hold in the hard years. Floods do come to a marriage: illness, poverty, grief, betrayal, the slow wearing of time. Real love is not extinguished by them, and many marriages that fail had let the fire burn low long before the floods came. But where a marriage was broken by a spouse's betrayal, desertion or abuse, the fault is not the faithful one's, and Christ's love for the wounded does not fail with it.

For the believer this is the settled ground of everything. Nothing will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:39). Having loved his own, he loved them to the end (John 13:1).

Love cannot be bought. A man who tried to purchase it with everything he owned would only show that he did not know what love is. It can only be given and received.

Which is why the gospel is not a transaction. No one buys God's love; it is given. And the only right response is the merchant's who found one pearl of great value and sold all that he had and bought it (Matt 13:46): not paying for love, but letting go of everything else for the sake of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Vineyard and the Final Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Her brothers ask what to do for their little sister (vv. 8-9). I was a wall, she answers, and she found peace in his eyes (v. 10). Solomon may keep his rented vineyard; her own is before her (vv. 11-12). He asks to hear her voice, and she calls, Make haste, my beloved (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Purity kept, love owned and not sold, and a last call for the beloved to come.

verseByVerse.quote: We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for? If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver, but if she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other voices now: her brothers, probably the same brothers who made her work the vineyards in 1:6, asking what to do for a younger sister when a suitor comes. If she proves a wall, keeping herself, they will crown it with silver. If a door, open to anyone, they will board her up. Their instinct is protection.

Parents and churches still face this question: what shall we do for the young, before they are spoken for? The Song's answer is neither neglect nor imprisonment, but preparation and honour. The aim is not merely to prevent something but to keep something for its time, so that it can be given whole. For this is the will of God, your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3), and the God who wills it is the one who sanctifies by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: I was a wall, and my breasts were like towers; then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answers for herself: she kept herself, and has not been a door open to everyone. Finds may be rendered "brings out" (ESV note): she found peace, or she brought peace to him. Both are true of a faithful wife.

She does not say, I was a wall, so I missed out. The woman who kept the gate locked is the woman of chapters 4 to 7, who knows love at its richest. Purity is not the enemy of passion. It is its protection.

For those who cannot say I was a wall, the gospel has a word. Christ makes the unclean clean, and presents his bride without blemish (Eph 5:27). No past puts a person beyond that mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard to keepers; each one was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A vineyard let out to tenants for a thousand pieces of silver: love as an estate managed for profit. Solomon had vineyards of that kind. Scripture records his seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines plainly and says they turned his heart away (1 Kgs 11:3–4). It reports polygamy without approving it, and the Song's own picture is one man and one woman, each the other's only one (6:3, 9).

And the bride speaks with quiet magnificence: keep your thousand, Solomon. She has one vineyard, her own love and her own husband, and she would not trade it for a royal estate.

Remember how she began: they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept! (1:6). The book that opened with a woman who had no vineyard of her own ends with her holding it, worth more to her than everything Solomon owns. One faithful marriage is richer than a kingdom of arrangements.
verseByVerse.note: Baal-hamon is otherwise unknown. A thousand pieces of silver was a great sum.

verseByVerse.quote: O you who dwell in the gardens, with companions listening for your voice; let me hear it. Make haste, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bridegroom's almost last words ask to hear her voice, as in 2:14. Of everything he could ask for, he asks for her speech. Love never tires of the beloved's voice.

And the bride has the last word, as she had the first (1:2). It is not a conclusion but a call: come quickly, like a young stag over the fragrant hills. The Song ends in longing, the lovers still reaching for each other. That is honest. This side of eternity love is never finished; it always wants more.

And the Bible ends the same way. The Spirit and the Bride say to the Bridegroom, Come (Rev 22:17), and he answers, Surely I am coming soon, and the church replies, Come, Lord Jesus! (Rev 22:20). The last prayer of the Song and the last prayer of Scripture are the same prayer. Whoever has learned to say Make haste, my beloved to a husband or a wife has learned something of what it means to wait for Christ; and whoever has learned to say it to Christ has found the love that is strong as death, and stronger.

8.title: Love Is Strong as Death
8.overview: The last chapter gathers up the whole Song. The lovers' embrace and the warning not to awaken love too soon return one last time (vv. 1-4). Then comes the summit of the book, where love is called strong as death and its flame the very flame of the LORD (vv. 5-7). The bride looks back on the purity she kept and the vineyard that is her own, and the Song closes not with an ending but with a call: Make haste, my beloved (vv. 8-14).
8.theology:
Love is to be guarded until its time (v. 4), and it must be guarded because it is strong as death and exclusive by nature (v. 6). Its flame is kindled by God himself, probably the one mention of the LORD in the book (v. 6; 1 John 4:19).

Love cannot be drowned or bought (v. 7): Christ's love for his people cannot be separated from them (Rom 8:39; John 13:1), and it is given, never purchased (Matt 13:46). Purity kept is honoured and brings peace (vv. 9-10; 1 Thess 4:3), and where it was not kept, Christ still presents his bride without blemish (Eph 5:27).

The Song ends in longing for the beloved to come, as Scripture ends with the Bride calling the Bridegroom (vv. 13-14; Rev 22:17, 20).
8.examples: An elderly couple walking slowly home from church, one leaning on the other, is the picture of verse 5. A wedding ring worn for fifty years is a seal set on the arm. And a man who tried to buy love with everything he owned would only prove he had never known it.
